posts.location: Renna's stall at the far end of the waygate marketplace crescent — dark-green oilcloth awning, early afternoon spring light, the boar tusks now on her bench and the commission formally recorded.
posts.narration:
Renna is bent over the bench recording the metal preference when Silas speaks. He does not speak to her. He speaks to Pell — or rather, he opens something toward Pell, and the words are only the surface of it.

"May I convey some things to you," he says, "to help you understand how to shape what you will make?"

He uses Order-Sense the way a man holds a door open — not to show the room, but to let the light through it. He finds the design Pell has in him: the morning on the ridge before the boar came, the cold working up through the mud into his knees, the way she stood three steps off his right shoulder without being asked because she had already read the ground and known where to be. He finds the boar — not the danger of it, but the weight of the moment just before it moved, when they were two people who had not yet said anything plainly and the world held them in that suspension. He finds the kill itself: not a proud thing, but a real one, taken cleanly and together, the first hard thing they did as a pair. He finds the walk back after, when the carcass was slung and neither of them spoke because neither of them needed to. He finds the tusks on the bench in front of them right…

posts.location: Frost-hard clearing two hundred yards north-and-west of the made gate — dead birch and alder at the edges, early-spring dawn, flat pale light. The wolverine's flesh has been eased away; the skeletal frame of Logana stands at the base of the downed tree, four-footed and still.
posts.narration:
You look at the wolverine and know what you are about to do before you have decided it. The Attended End is still open — you have not closed it — and through that open door you can see the full architecture of what remains: bone that held eleven years of hard country, joints that never failed her, a skeleton that the Zone made denser and more deliberate than it should be. You read the sequence before you begin. Flesh decays in a direction. Bone wards in another. You can hold both at once if you are careful.

The first step is Deathsense, run wide — and the full design of the ending lays itself out plain. You know exactly where each bone seats, how the joints will hold when the flesh is gone, where the warding must go to make a guardian rather than a ruin. Order-Sense confirms the design as you build it in your mind. The relay node in the hollow pulses faint and steady beneath the tree roots, and you feel the clearing's lattice-work recognize what you are attempting. The second step is Palework, turned gentle — easing the flesh toward its own ending, not tearing, not forcing. It goes cleanly. The bone emerges pale and dense and exactly as the reading promised.

The warding is where it wrinkles. You lay the guardian-purpose into the bones with the care the craft requires, but the relay node beneath the tree takes an interest it was not asked for — a thread of the Zone's lattice seats itself into the ward alongside your own, and the intention you named arrives in the structure alongside something older and less clear. It is not wrong. It is not entirely yours. You hold it, finish the binding, and call it a complication, not a failure.

Shadow Work comes next — you draw dark into the bone-frame, give it the shape of sustained purpose, and then you reach for the radiant binding that will make it move. The four crafts braid into something that should not exist in an ordinary clearing: the bones rise, settle onto four feet, and stand. They are still. They are waiting. Huginn, who has not moved from the flat stone at the edge of the clearing, turns its head away and then back, the way it does when it is reconsidering something.

You speak her name last. Logana. The adaptation carries — the name seats into the ward the way the Weirmark seated into the gate, and the skeletal wolverine turns her head toward the relay node, then back toward you, then toward the line of trees to the south where Pell and Veth are waiting. Not obedient. Aware. The Zone-thread in the warding has made her partly the Zone's creature, and partly yours, and the two intentions sit in her frame without fighting. That is the best you were going to get here, and it is enough. Veth's voice carries across two hundred yards of Zone ground, measured and plain: still moving, keep pace.

*✦ A braid forms — **Deathsense and Palework** become **The Hollowing Sight**.*

posts.location: A lean-to shelter at the edge of The Thinning settlement, early morning, light bent and strange. The open doorway frames the thin place — trees, grass, the waygate clearing. The air tastes of copper and honeysuckle. Spring melt.
posts.narration:
You push yourself up on your elbows and follow Boo's unblinking stare into the space between the trees.

At first there is nothing — just the bent light, the copper taste, the settlement's sounds distant behind you. Then your eyes adjust, and the space resolves into something that was ALWAYS there and your waking mind had simply refused to hold it.

A figure stands in the thin place where the trees open onto the waygate clearing. They are not quite solid. Light passes through them the way light passes through water — bent, but moving. Their shape is human enough to recognize and wrong enough to make your breath catch: too many joints in the arms, a posture that suggests they are standing and falling simultaneously, a face that shifts when you look at it directly — not changing, but revealing, layer by layer, that there was always more to see.

Boo's ears — both of them, though you were certain a moment ago there was only one — rotate toward you. A statement: *This one came through.*

The figure does not move. Does not seem to see you. But the air around them hums with the same tone that woke you this morning, and you understand with sudden clarity that they are *reading* the valley the way you read a page — taking in everything at once, learning the shape of it. The veil is not just thin here. It is open. And something on the other side has noticed that it can step through.

posts.location: The Common Table, long communal hall 140 m from the Crossing's centre. Midday, early spring. Pale cold light, mud on the floor, close-packed benches, boiled-herb smell.
posts.narration:
You close your eyes for a moment — not long, just long enough to let the Common Table's noise drop to background. The near-fight's residue is still in your chest, that particular tightness, but you breathe past it and reach.

This time something comes.

Not a full vision — not the wide, slow, river-of-images kind that sometimes keeps you rooted in place for a minute and a half while everyone around you pretends not to stare. This is a fragment. A single still image, clear and cold: a road running outward from the Crossing, the light on it wrong — too bright on one side, shadow pooling on the other where shadow has no cause to pool. Two figures walking it. One of them has no face in the image, only a direction. The other is Brynjar, unmistakably, though you have not known him long enough to say how you know it.

You speak it aloud, low and level, not performing, just reporting: "A road running outward. Light and shadow both wrong on it, each keeping to its side. You are on the road. Someone walks beside you whose face the vision does not show me. I don't know yet if that is a good thing." You pause. "It arrived this time. Make of it what you will."

posts.location: The Crow and Thistle, small upstairs room, second door on the left. Midday spring light through the shutter-crack. Gear dry on the peg. Common room sounds — scraping benches, low voices, something frying — rising from below.
posts.narration:
The dream takes you without asking, the way it always does.

One moment there is nothing — the blank, merciful dark of exhausted sleep — and then the longhouse closes around you like a fist. Smoke first, always smoke, the thick resinous kind that gets behind your eyes and stays there. Then the shouting, voices you cannot place anymore, and underneath it all the crack of a roof-beam giving way, a sound like a spine breaking, and the orange light painting everything the colour of embers and anger. Fire inside. Fire where there should only be hearthlight and the smell of your mother's cooking, and instead it is this, it is always this.

You move the way you moved then. Fast. Low. Your body remembers even when your mind does not want to. The axe is already in your hand — you never had to think about it, even at seventeen, even terrified — and the smoke parts just enough to show you one of Kjotve's men coming through it like something dredged up from the bottom of the sea. Broad-shouldered. A cut splitting the skin above one eye, the blood already black in the firelight. He sees you. He opens his mouth.

You swing.

The axe finds him with a weight and a sound you have never been able to forget no matter how many years of trying, and his face is the last clear thing in the whole burning world — that particular expression, that flash of something almost like surprise — before the longhouse tilts sideways beneath your feet as though the earth itself is disgusted with what it has witnessed. And then your father's voice. Just once. Your name, spoken from somewhere so far away that reaching it would mean crossing an ocean you do not have the years to cross anymore, and the sound of it tears something loose in your chest the way it does every time.

Then Kjotve's laugh, low and satisfied and obscene.

Then the ocean, sudden and cold and immense, right there where the door used to be.

Then the place where Andyr was standing, which is only empty air.

You come up out of it swinging.

The shout fills the room before you know you've made it, raw and shapeless, the kind of sound that belongs in burning places and not in small rented rooms above a tavern. Your hand goes straight for your hip, fingers finding the axe frog on pure reflex — and there is nothing. Just wool. Just the rough weave of the blanket twisted around your legs, and your own heart trying to get out through your sternum, and the dark.

You sit with it for a moment. The dark resolves slowly into the familiar. Straw. Rough-hewn timber. The smell of tallow candles long since burned down to nothing and old wood that has absorbed twenty winters of woodsmoke and spilled ale. The weak, pale light of a spring morning bleeding through the gap in the shutters, thin as watered milk, enough to tell you the world is still here. You are in the second-door room at the Crow and Thistle. The floor is not on fire. No one is laughing.

Freki is already on his feet.

He stands at the foot of the bed the way he always does when you come up from the bad ones — not startled, not whining, not doing any of the anxious things a lesser animal might do. Just watching. Those yellow-green eyes are steady in the dimness, ears lifted, the great head tilted perhaps two degrees in what you have come to understand as his version of a question. He reads you the way a sailor reads weather: patiently, without judgment, waiting to know what kind of thing this is going to be. After a moment, having apparently decided, he takes two deliberate steps forward across the straw-scattered boards and presses the flat of his jaw against your knee.

Just weight. Just the warmth of him, solid and real and present.

You breathe.

In. Out. The tightness in your chest begins, slowly, to loosen its grip.

The axe is exactly where you left it — leaned against the wall within arm's reach, as it always is, as it will be in every room you sleep in for the rest of your life. You reach for it before you reach for anything else. The haft settles into your palm with the particular ease of a thing that has been held ten thousand times, the wood worn smooth in exactly the places where your grip sits, polished not by craft but by years. You turn it once, slowly, feeling the balance of it, the familiar weight redistributing itself through your wrist and forearm. Proof. Evidence. You are here. You are holding the axe. You are not seventeen, and the longhouse is ash, and whatever you are now, you are still standing.

You set it on the bed and dress in the cool dimness. Boots first, the leather still faintly stiff from yesterday's wet — laced tight, stomped down until they seat properly. Belt. Tunic. The ordinary ritual of putting yourself back together, layer by layer, until the thing that woke up screaming is tucked back where it belongs and something more functional has taken its place. The axe drops into its frog with the small, solid click that has closed a thousand mornings just like this one. Shield off the wall, arm through the strap — the familiar weight settling across your back like a hand on the shoulder — and you are, in some recognizable sense, yourself again.

The morning has dried your gear while you slept. That much, at least, it gave you.

From below, the common room is already alive. The scrape of a bench across stone flags. A low voice placing an order, unhurried. And riding above it all, rich enough to make your empty stomach clench with want: something frying in an iron pan, fat and savoury, the smell curling up through the floorboards like an invitation. You glance at the thin light still seeping through the shutters and make your best reckoning. Midday, near enough. You slept far longer than you meant to.

You give Freki's ears one brief, rough pass with your knuckles — he leans into it, eyes briefly closing — and then you go to meet the day.

posts.location: The Made Gate clearing in full night—the circle fully claimed and marked, four unmarked pole-stations at cardinal points, the central shrine a simple unadorned stone at the heart. The Made Gate itself stands to the south, shadow-warded and sealed. Stars visible overhead; the moorland stretches dark in all directions.
posts.narration:
The moorland dark presses close around you when you turn from the shrine's unmarked heart. There is no light here but what the sky relinquishes — that thin, bled-out copper bleeding westward behind clouds that move like slow thought. You feel the emptiness of the circle at your back, the four cardinal stations standing open in their patient distances, and something in your chest has gone quiet, the way a bell goes quiet after its last long ringing — not absence, but a different kind of presence.

You raise your hand toward the gate-post.

"Come," you say, and the moorland carries it — no echo, no distortion, just your voice laid flat across the dark like a lamp set in a window. "Witness this. The ending of the pull — not one pole winning, but both falling still. Come and see what comes after."

Huginn does not move at first.

She is a shape against the post's shadow, and her stillness is the particular stillness of something very old deciding whether a thing is worth its attention. One eye — that eye, the one that holds too much calm in it, the kind of calm that has watched cities become meadows — fixes on you across the distance. The wind moves between you. The heather bends and straightens. Somewhere far off a curlew calls and falls silent, as if it, too, is listening for her answer.

Then she spreads her wings.

The sound is wrong in the most precise way. You know the sound of feathers — the hollow percussion of air being caught and thrown — but this is something older asserting itself through the same motion, the way a tide asserts itself through the rolling of a single stone. She launches from the post with a downstroke that carries more weight than her body should contain, and she crosses the dark between you in the time it takes to breathe once, and when she lands the displacement of her passage moves against your face like the closing of a great book.

She folds her wings.

She is not entirely a bird anymore.

She is a woman, and she is tall, and the grey of her is not the grey of ash so much as it is the grey of river stone that has been under moving water for longer than the riverbank remembers. Her hands hang steady at her sides — hands that have seen use, weathered and deliberate. Her face is the face of someone who has learned that patience is not a virtue but a condition, like gravity. And the eye is the same. That eye. The full weight of whatever she is arrives through it and settles over you like a door swung shut in a quiet room — not threatening, simply final.

"I have watched endings," she says. Her voice is gravel worn smooth by water — not soft, not gentle, but all the roughness rounded to something you can hold without cutting yourself. "I have not watched *this* before."

The circle holds around you both. The four pole-stations stand at their cardinal points — north, east, south, west — open and unmarked and waiting in the way that only truly open things can wait, without hunger, without agenda. The central shrine rises unadorned behind you, and the last light from the western sky catches it in a way that makes it look briefly like something that has always been here and always will be, regardless of who comes to tend it. Behind it, the Made Gate stands shadow-dark and entirely real — not looming, not menacing, but present the way a fact is present, patient and indifferent to whether you find it convenient.

Marrow studies you.

"Tell me what you mean by true path," she says, and it is not a question. It is an instruction issued by a warden who has spent a very long time learning the difference between what people say and what they mean, and who will feel the gap between them like a fault-line underfoot if you leave one. The eye does not soften. The hands do not move. She is giving you her full precision, and she expects yours in return.
